items.stem:
On the basis of reactivity metals are grouped into three categories: (i) Metals of low reactivity (ii) Metals of medium reactivity (iii) Metals of high reactivity. Therefore metals are extracted in pure form from their ores on the basis of their chemical properties. Metals of high reactivity are extracted from their ores by electrolysis of the molten ore. Metals of low reactivity are extracted from their sulphide ores, which are converted into their oxides. The oxides of these metals are reduced to metals by simple heating.
(a) Name the process of reduction used for a metal that gives vigorous reaction with air and water both.
(b) Carbon cannot be used as a reducing agent to obtain aluminium from its oxide? Why?
(c) Describe briefly the method to obtain mercury from cinnabar. Write the chemical equation for the reactions involved in the process.
(d) Differentiate between roasting and calcination giving chemical equation for each.
items.answer:
(a) Electrolytic reduction. The metal is likely to be sodium (Na). It has very high affinity for oxygen, so reducing agents like carbon and aluminium cannot be used.
(b) Because aluminium has a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has, therefore carbon cannot reduce alumina (Al₂O₃) to aluminium.
(c) Cinnabar (HgS — mercury(II) sulphide or mercury sulphide) is an ore of mercury. It is heated in air to give mercuric oxide (HgO). Mercuric oxide is further heated to get mercury. The reactions involved are:
2HgS(s) + 3O₂ →(heat) 2HgO(s) + 2SO₂(g)
2HgO(s) →(heat) 2Hg(s) + O₂(g)
(d) Calcination is defined as the process of converting an ore into an oxide by heating it strongly. The ore is heated below its melting point either in the absence of air or in a limited supply of air, e.g. ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.
Roasting is a process of metallurgy where an ore is converted into its oxide by heating it below its melting point in the presence of excess air. An example of roasting is when zinc sulphide is converted into zinc oxide: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂.

items.stem: Discuss the physical properties of non-metals.
items.answer:
Physical properties of non-metals are the following:
(i) Non-metals are brittle: They break into pieces when hammered or stretched, i.e. they are not malleable.
(ii) Non-metals are non-ductile: These cannot be drawn into wires.
(iii) Non-metals are bad conductors of heat and electricity: Non-metals do not have free electrons. There is one exception, graphite, which is a good conductor of heat and electricity.
(iv) Non-metals are non-lustrous and cannot be polished: The exceptions are graphite and iodine, which are lustrous.
(v) Non-metals are generally soft: Except diamond (an allotropic form of carbon), which is the hardest substance known, non-metals are soft.
(vi) Non-metals generally have low melting and boiling points: Except graphite, which has a high melting point, non-metals have weak intramolecular force.
(vii) Non-metals have low densities: Most non-metals are light.

items.stem: Discuss the exceptions in the properties of metals and non-metals.
items.answer:
(i) All metals except mercury exist as solids at room temperature. Metals have high melting points, but gallium and caesium have very low melting points. These two metals will melt if they are kept on the palm.
(ii) Iodine is a non-metal but it is lustrous.
(iii) Carbon is a non-metal that can exist in different forms. Each form is called an allotrope. Diamond, an allotrope of carbon, is the hardest natural substance known and has very high melting and boiling points. Graphite, another allotrope of carbon, is a conductor of electricity.
(iv) Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are so soft that they can be cut with a knife. They have low densities and low melting points.

items.stem: In what forms are metals found in nature? With the help of examples explain how metals react with oxygen, water and dilute acids. Also write chemical equations for the reactions.
items.answer:
(i) Metals are found in the form of both the free and the combined state.
(ii) Reaction of metals with oxygen: All metals combine with oxygen and form metal oxides. For example, when copper is heated in air it combines with oxygen and forms copper oxide:
2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO
Reaction of metals with water: Metals like sodium react with cold water, magnesium reacts with hot water and iron reacts with steam.
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Reaction of metals with acids: Metals react with acids and form salt and hydrogen gas. For example, magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and forms magnesium chloride and hydrogen:
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

items.stem:
Give reason for the following:
(i) Gold and platinum are used in jewellery.
(ii) Copper cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
(iii) Stainless steel does not rust easily.
(iv) Metals can be given different shapes according to our needs.
(v) Zinc does not give hydrogen gas on reacting with HNO₃.
items.answer:
(i) Gold and silver are shiny and unreactive, so they are used in jewellery.
(ii) Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.
(iii) Stainless steel is an alloy, so it does not rust easily.
(iv) Metals are malleable and ductile, so they can take different shapes as we wish.
(v) Since HNO₃ is a strong oxidising agent, it oxidises the H₂ formed to H₂O and itself gets reduced to one of the oxides of nitrogen.
items.ocr: Part (i) of the question names gold and platinum but the printed solution answers for 'Gold and silver' — solution text kept as printed and the mismatch recorded here. items.stem:
(a) Describe the steps associated with extraction of copper from its sulphide ore.
(b) How is impure copper purified by electrolytic refining?
or
(a) How is copper obtained from its sulphide ore? Write balanced chemical equations.
(b) Give the electrolytic refining of impure copper with diagram.
items.answer:
(a) Copper is obtained from its sulphide ore Cu₂S by heating it strongly in air:
2Cu₂S(s) + 3O₂ →(Δ) 2Cu₂O(s) + 2SO₂(g)
2Cu₂O + Cu₂S →(Δ) 6Cu(s) + SO₂(g)
(b) The printed solution answers this part with a labelled diagram of the electrolytic refining of copper: a thick block of impure copper forms the anode, a thin strip of pure copper forms the cathode and acidified copper sulphate solution is the electrolyte. On passing electric current, copper dissolves from the anode into the solution and an equivalent amount of pure copper is deposited on the cathode, while the insoluble impurities settle below the anode as anode mud.

items.stem:
A metal E is stored under kerosene. When a small piece of it is left open in the air, it catches fire. When the product formed is dissolved in water it turns red litmus to blue.
(i) Name the metal E.
(ii) Write the chemical equation for the reaction when it is exposed to air and when the product is dissolved in water.
(iii) Explain the process by which the metal is obtained from its molten chloride.
items.answer:
(i) Metal E is sodium.
(ii) 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH
(iii) Electrolysis of the molten metal chloride (NaCl) gives the pure metal (Na). In this process, Na is deposited at the cathode:
Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
Cl₂ is liberated at the anode:
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
items.ocr: The printed solution repeats '4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O' twice; the second line must be the dissolution of the product in water, restored as Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH to match part (ii) of the question. LaTeX rewritten in Unicode.

items.stem:
A metal M found in nature as sulphide ore (MS) is one of the good conductors of heat and electricity and is used in making electric wires.
(i) Identify the metal M.
(ii) Write the balanced chemical equations involved in the process of extraction of the metal.
(iii) Draw a labelled diagram of electrolytic refining of the metal.
items.answer:
(i) Metal M is copper.
(ii) (a) 2Cu₂S(s) + 3O₂(g) →(heating) 2Cu₂O(s) + 2SO₂(g)
(b) 2Cu₂O(s) + Cu₂S(s) →(heating) 6Cu(s) + SO₂(g)

items.stem: Write the names and symbols of two most reactive metals. Explain by drawing electronic structure how any one of the two metals reacts with a halogen. State any two physical properties of the compound formed.
items.answer:
(i) The two most reactive metals are sodium (Na) and potassium (K).
(ii) The printed solution shows the electron-dot/shell structures: sodium (2,8,1) transfers its single valence electron to a chlorine atom (2,8,7). Sodium then becomes Na⁺ (2,8) and chlorine becomes Cl⁻ (2,8,8); both attain the stable noble-gas configuration and are held together by electrostatic attraction as Na⁺Cl⁻.
(iii) Properties of the compound NaCl (or KCl):
(a) It has a high melting point and boiling point.
(b) It conducts electricity in the molten state or in solution and is soluble in water.

items.stem:
(i) Design an activity to show the conditions needed for iron nails to rust.
(ii) Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
items.answer:
(i) Take three test tubes and place clean iron nails in each of them. Label these test tubes A, B and C. Pour some water in test tube A and cork it. Pour boiled distilled water in test tube B, then pour about 1 mL oil and cork it — the oil will float on the water and prevent air from entering. Put some anhydrous calcium chloride in test tube C and cork it; anhydrous calcium chloride will absorb the moisture, if any, from the air. Leave these test tubes for a few days and then observe.
In tube B there is no air in the water, so the nails do not rust. In tube C the air is dry and the nails do not rust. We will observe that the nails rust in test tube A but they do not rust in test tubes B and C. In test tube A the nails are exposed to both air and water; in test tube B the nails are exposed to only water, whereas in test tube C the nails are exposed to only dry air. This shows that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.
(ii) Rusting of iron can be prevented by painting the surface of the iron object; as a result, oxygen and moisture of the atmosphere do not come in direct contact with the surface of the iron.

items.stem:
(a) All ores are minerals but all minerals are not ores. Justify the statement.
(b) What is galvanisation?
(c) Explain roasting with the help of a reaction.
(d) What do you mean by amalgam?
items.answer:
(a) An ore is the mineral from which a metal can be profitably or economically extracted. A metal cannot be extracted profitably from every mineral, so all minerals are not ores.
(b) Galvanisation is a process of coating a thin layer of zinc over iron sheets.
(c) Roasting is the process of heating a sulphide ore at high temperature in excess of oxygen. Example: 2ZnS + 3O₂ →(Heat) 2ZnO + 2SO₂
(d) If one of the metals in an alloy is mercury, then the alloy is known as an amalgam.

items.stem: What are alloys? How are they made? Name the constituents and uses of brass, bronze and solder.
items.answer:
A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal, is known as an alloy. An alloy is prepared by (i) melting the primary metal, and (ii) dissolving the other elements in it in a definite proportion and cooling to room temperature.
AlloyConstituentUses
BrassCu and Znin making utensils
BronzeCu and Snmarking statue medal
SolderPb and Snin soldering

items.stem:
(a) Define corrosion.
(b) What is corrosion of iron called?
(c) How will you recognise the corrosion of silver?
(d) Why is corrosion of iron a serious problem?
(e) How can we prevent corrosion of iron?
items.answer:
(a) It is a process in which a metal reacts with substances present in air to form surface compounds.
(b) Rusting.
(c) By a black layer on its surface due to the formation of Ag₂S.
(d) It makes the metal weak and brittle, which is a serious problem.
(e) Oiling, painting, greasing, galvanisation and alloying can prevent iron from corrosion.

items.stem:
Explain the following:
(i) Metals at the top of the reactivity series do not occur in the free state in nature.
(ii) Finely powdered ore is mixed with a suitable oil and water in the concentration of a sulphide ore.
(iii) Sulphide ores need to be roasted after concentration.
(iv) Mercury can be obtained just by roasting the ore.
(v) Highly reactive metals are obtained by electrolytic reduction of their compounds.
items.answer:
(i) Metals at the top of the reactivity series are very reactive metals. They react with air, water and carbon dioxide to form their oxides, hydroxides and carbonates. Hence, they do not occur in the free state in nature.
(ii) The sulphide ore is wetted by pine oil and not by water. When the finely powdered ore mixed with the oil is agitated with water, the foam of the pine oil picks up the ore particles, which are thus separated from the impurities.
(iii) It is very difficult to extract a metal from its sulphide ore. On roasting, the sulphide ore is transformed into the oxide of the metal. This oxide can easily be reduced to the metal by heating it with coke or carbon monoxide.
(iv) Mercury is very low in the reactivity series, hence it is very inactive. When cinnabar (HgS), an ore of mercury, is heated in air, it is first converted into mercuric oxide (HgO), which is then reduced to mercury:
2HgS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2HgO(s) + 2SO₂(g)
2HgO(s) → 2Hg(l) + O₂(g)
(v) Highly reactive metals cannot be obtained from their compounds by heating with carbon, because these metals have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon has. However, in electrolytic reduction, a large amount of energy produced breaks up the bonds in the metal oxides.

items.stem:
(a) What is an ionic bond?
(b) How is an ionic bond formed?
(c) Write the formation of magnesium chloride.
items.answer:
(a) The chemical bond formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another is known as an ionic bond.
(b) An ionic bond is formed when one of the atoms can donate electrons to achieve the inert-gas electronic configuration and the other atom needs electrons to achieve the inert-gas electronic configuration. When a metal (usually 1, 2 or 3 electrons in the outermost shell) reacts with a non-metal (usually 5, 6 or 7 electrons in the outermost shell), transfer of electrons takes place from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms and an ionic bond is formed. There is a strong force of electrostatic attraction between the metallic cation and the non-metallic anion, which is responsible for the formation of the ionic bond.
(c) Formation of magnesium chloride (MgCl₂): The atomic number of magnesium is 12, so it has two electrons in its valence shell: ₁₂Mg → 2, 8, 2. Magnesium therefore has a tendency to lose the 2 valence electrons and in the process attains the electronic configuration of neon:
Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
Chlorine (atomic number 17) has 7 electrons in the valence shell. It has a tendency to gain one electron to complete its octet:
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Thus, when magnesium and chlorine are brought together, the magnesium atom transfers its two valence electrons to two chlorine atoms. In the process, both the atoms acquire the stable electronic configuration of the nearest inert gases. The positively charged magnesium ion Mg²⁺ and the negatively charged chloride ions Cl⁻ are now held together by the electrostatic force of attraction and form an ionic bond:
Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → Mg²⁺2Cl⁻ or MgCl₂
